content.question_text: What is a lambda expression?

core_requirements: A block of code that can be passed around
Can be executed later, once or multiple times
acceptable_variations: User's own phrasing of 'code as a value'

content.question_text: Write the basic syntax pattern of a lambda expression.

core_requirements: (parameter, parameter) -> expression
acceptable_variations: Any correctly shaped example using this pattern

content.question_text: What is required in a lambda expression when the logic after -> cannot fit into a single expression?

core_requirements: A block { } with explicit return statement(s)

content.question_text: On a basic level, what is a lambda expression made of?

core_requirements: A block of code
The specification of any variables/parameters that must be passed to it

content.question_text: How do you write a lambda expression that takes no parameters?

core_requirements: Supply empty parentheses, e.g. () -> ...

content.question_text: When can you omit the parameter types in a lambda expression?

core_requirements: When the compiler can infer the types from context (e.g. the target functional interface)

content.question_text: Give an example of a lambda assigned to a Comparator<String> variable where parameter types are omitted.

core_requirements: Comparator<String> byLength = (first, second) -> first.length() - second.length();
or equivalent valid example
acceptable_variations: Any correct Comparator<String> lambda without explicit types

content.question_text: When can you omit the parentheses around a lambda's parameter list entirely?

core_requirements: When the lambda has exactly one parameter with an inferred type

content.question_text: How do you denote a lambda parameter that is never used in the body?

core_requirements: Underscore: _

content.question_text: Do you ever specify the return type of a lambda expression? Why or why not?

core_requirements: Never explicitly specified
It is always inferred from context (the target functional interface's method)

content.question_text: Why is a lambda block invalid if it returns a value on some branches but not others (e.g. an if with a return in one branch and nothing in the other)?

core_requirements: It is illegal for a lambda expression's block body to return a value in some branches and not in others — all paths must consistently return or not return

content.question_text: What is a functional interface?

core_requirements: An interface with exactly one abstract method

content.question_text: What kind of interfaces can be used as the target type for a lambda expression?

core_requirements: Functional interfaces only

content.question_text: What does it mean that a lambda 'converts to' a functional interface when used as a method argument?

core_requirements: It means you can supply a whole lambda expression in place of a parameter of that functional interface type

content.question_text: Why should you generally use a purpose-built functional interface (like Comparator or Predicate) instead of a generic one (like BiFunction) when one is available?

core_requirements: Purpose-built interfaces carry semantic meaning (what the lambda is FOR), not just matching parameter/return shapes
APIs (e.g. Arrays.sort) require the specific interface type, not just a matching shape
acceptable_variations: Any explanation showing understanding that shape alone isn't enough — the declared interface type matters

content.question_text: What does it mean that method arguments are evaluated eagerly?

core_requirements: The arguments are computed/evaluated before the method is even called

content.question_text: Explain lazy evaluation in the context of lambdas.

core_requirements: Supplying a Supplier (or similar) as the parameter so the value is only computed when it's actually needed/used, not upfront

content.question_text: What is the job of the Supplier<T> interface?

core_requirements: To yield/produce a value of type T when its get() method is called

content.question_text: What is the job of the Predicate<T> interface?

core_requirements: Takes a value of type T and returns a boolean (a boolean-valued test)

content.question_text: When can you use a method reference instead of a full lambda expression?

core_requirements: When the lambda's entire body would just be calling one existing method whose signature matches what the functional interface requires

content.question_text: What operator/syntax denotes a method reference?
List the four forms a method reference can take.

core_requirements: Class::staticMethod
Class::instanceMethod (called on the first parameter)
object::instanceMethod (called on an existing object)
Class::new (constructor reference)
acceptable_variations: Reasonable rewording of each, as long as all 4 distinct forms are present

content.question_text: Can you use this:: and super:: as method references?

core_requirements: Yes

content.question_text: When a class has multiple overloaded constructors and you use a constructor reference (Class::new), how does Java determine which constructor is actually called?

core_requirements: Java picks the constructor whose parameter types match the target functional interface's method signature

content.question_text: For a constructor reference like Person::new to match a functional interface, must the interface's parameter types match Person's constructor, or must the interface's return type match Person? Which one is it?

core_requirements: The functional interface's return type must match the constructed class (Person)
AND the interface's parameter types must match one of the constructors' parameter lists — both conditions apply, but the key distinguishing point is the RETURN type equals the class

content.question_text: What are the three ingredients of a lambda expression?

core_requirements: A block of code
Parameters
Values for free variables

content.question_text: What is a free variable?

core_requirements: A variable that is neither a parameter nor defined inside the lambda's code

content.question_text: What is the technical term for a block of code together with the values of its free variables?

core_requirements: Closure

content.question_text: What is the restriction on free variables used inside a lambda expression?

core_requirements: The lambda cannot mutate them, and cannot reference variables that are mutated outside the lambda (they must be effectively final)

content.question_text: What do you call it when the value of a free variable is used inside a lambda expression?

core_requirements: The value is said to be 'captured'

content.question_text: What does it mean for a variable to be 'effectively final'?

core_requirements: Its value is never reassigned after it has been initialized

content.question_text: Does a lambda expression have its own 'this' reference? Explain what 'this' refers to inside a lambda.

core_requirements: No, a lambda does not have its own this
'this' inside a lambda refers to the this of the enclosing method/scope, not the lambda itself

content.question_text: Can a lambda expression access a field from its enclosing class?

core_requirements: Yes

content.question_text: What does the static Comparator.comparing() method do, and what is the role of the function you pass into it?

core_requirements: comparing() builds a full Comparator for you
The passed-in function is a 'key extractor' — it pulls out the specific field/value from each object to compare by
The actual comparison is then done using that extracted key's natural ordering

content.question_text: What does thenComparing() do when chained after Comparator.comparing()?

core_requirements: Provides a secondary comparison key used to break ties when the primary comparison is equal
